title: Serving a Model on EC2 GPUs
desc: From an empty AWS account to a live, OpenAI-compatible vLLM endpoint on a real GPU box — instance selection, SSH, environment setup, systemd, and testing the endpoint end to end.
content:
Everything in Day 1 and Day 2 was math and architecture. Today you rent a GPU, SSH into it, and get a model answering HTTP requests. This is the lesson to keep open in a second tab while you actually do it — every command here is meant to be copy-pasted, not just read.

🔑
Today's outcome
By the end you'll have: 1) a GPU EC2 instance running, 2) vLLM serving a model on an OpenAI-compatible endpoint, 3) that server surviving SSH disconnects and reboots via systemd, and 4) a working curl/Python request hitting it from your laptop.

Step 1 — Pick an Instance Type

AWS's GPU instances split into two families: G-series (inference-oriented, cheaper) and P-series (training-oriented, more VRAM and interconnect bandwidth, expensive). For serving a single 7-8B model, you almost never need a P-series instance.

InstanceGPUVRAMGood for
g5.xlarge1x NVIDIA A10G24 GB7-8B model, fp16/bf16, single request stream
g6.xlarge1x NVIDIA L424 GBSame class as g5, newer generation, better perf/$ for inference
g5.12xlarge4x NVIDIA A10G96 GB13-34B model, or a 7-8B model with high concurrency + tensor parallel
p4d.24xlarge8x NVIDIA A100320 GB (40GB x8)70B+ model serving, fine-tuning at scale
p5.48xlarge8x NVIDIA H100640 GBLargest models, highest-throughput serving, training
💵
Don't trust a memorized number for price
On-demand GPU pricing changes with region, and spot pricing can be 60-90% cheaper than on-demand for the exact same hardware. Always check the live EC2 On-Demand Pricing page for your region before committing a budget number — a course chapter's number will be stale within months.

Use the back-of-envelope math from Day 1 to check VRAM fits before you launch: a 7B model in bf16 needs ~14 GB just for weights, leaving headroom on a 24 GB card for KV cache — fine for moderate concurrency, tight for high concurrency.

Step 2 — Launch the Instance

Two choices matter more than the others when you launch:

  • AMI: use an AWS Deep Learning AMI (DLAMI) — it ships with the NVIDIA driver, CUDA, cuDNN, and a ready-made PyTorch virtual environment already installed. Skipping this means fighting driver installs by hand.
  • Security group: you need inbound TCP 22 (SSH, restricted to your IP) and inbound TCP 8000 (the vLLM server port, restricted to your IP or your VPN/office CIDR — never 0.0.0.0/0 for a raw, unauthenticated model endpoint).
Shell · launch from the AWS CLI
# Launch a g5.xlarge with a recent Deep Learning AMI (look up the current AMI ID
# for your region in the DLAMI docs before running this)
aws ec2 run-instances \
  --image-id ami-0XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX \
  --instance-type g5.xlarge \
  --key-name my-key \
  --security-group-ids sg-0XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX \
  --block-device-mappings '[{"DeviceName":"/dev/sda1","Ebs":{"VolumeSize":100}}]' \
  --count 1

100 GB of disk is a reasonable floor — model weights for a 7-8B model in safetensors run 15-30 GB, and you'll want room for a second model or Docker layers.

Step 3 — SSH In

Once the instance is running and has a public IP (check the console or aws ec2 describe-instances), connect exactly the way you would to any Ubuntu box:

Shell · connect and sanity-check the GPU
ssh -i ~/.ssh/my-key.pem ubuntu@1.2.3.4

# step 1: land in your home dir
cd ~

# step 2: confirm the driver + GPU are visible before installing anything else
nvidia-smi
⚠️
If nvidia-smi fails
Stop here. A DLAMI should have the driver pre-installed — if it isn't showing your GPU, you likely picked a non-GPU AMI or a non-GPU instance type. Don't proceed to installing vLLM on a box that can't see a GPU; you'll just get confusing CPU-fallback errors an hour from now.

Step 4 — Environment Setup

The DLAMI's PyTorch venv already has CUDA-matched torch installed. Activate it, then install vLLM on top:

Shell · activate env, install vLLM, verify CUDA
# DLAMI ships a ready-made venv (path varies by DLAMI version — check
# /opt/ or ~/ if this path doesn't exist on your image)
source /opt/pytorch/bin/activate

pip install vllm

# confirm torch sees the GPU inside the venv
python3 -c "import torch; print(torch.cuda.is_available(), torch.cuda.get_device_name(0))"

If you'd rather isolate vLLM in its own environment instead of the DLAMI's default venv, a plain python3 -m venv ~/vllm-env && source ~/vllm-env/bin/activate works too — just make sure the venv's torch build matches the installed CUDA version.

Step 5 — Download a Model and Start the Server

Shell · authenticate to Hugging Face and pull weights
export HF_TOKEN=hf_xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx

huggingface-cli download meta-llama/Meta-Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct \
  --local-dir ~/models/llama-3.1-8b-instruct
Shell · start vLLM's OpenAI-compatible server, bound for external access
vllm serve ~/models/llama-3.1-8b-instruct \
  --served-model-name llama-3.1-8b \
  --dtype bfloat16 \
  --max-model-len 8192 \
  --gpu-memory-utilization 0.90 \
  --host 0.0.0.0 \
  --port 8000 \
  --api-key token-abc123
💡
Why --host 0.0.0.0 and a security group, not one or the other
vLLM defaults to binding localhost, which only accepts connections from inside the box itself. --host 0.0.0.0 tells it to accept connections on every network interface — but that alone doesn't expose it to the internet. The EC2 security group is the actual firewall; it must separately allow inbound traffic on port 8000. You need both: the app listening on the right interface, and the network permitting traffic to reach it. Always pass --api-key too — an unauthenticated model endpoint on the open internet gets found and abused within hours.

Step 6 — Keep It Alive

Running the command above directly in your SSH session works for a five-minute test, but the process dies the moment you disconnect. Two options, in order of maturity:

Quick test: tmux

Shell · survive a dropped SSH session
tmux new -s vllm
# run the vllm serve command inside this session
# detach with Ctrl-b then d — the process keeps running
# reattach later with:
tmux attach -t vllm

Production path: systemd

A systemd unit restarts the server automatically on crash or reboot, and gives you journalctl for logs — the same operational pattern used for any long-running Linux service.

ini · /etc/systemd/system/vllm.service
[Unit]
Description=vLLM OpenAI-compatible server
After=network.target

[Service]
Type=simple
User=ubuntu
Environment="HF_TOKEN=hf_xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx"
WorkingDirectory=/home/ubuntu
ExecStart=/opt/pytorch/bin/vllm serve /home/ubuntu/models/llama-3.1-8b-instruct \
  --served-model-name llama-3.1-8b \
  --dtype bfloat16 \
  --max-model-len 8192 \
  --gpu-memory-utilization 0.90 \
  --host 0.0.0.0 \
  --port 8000 \
  --api-key token-abc123
Restart=on-failure
RestartSec=5

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target
Shell · enable and start the service
sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl enable vllm
sudo systemctl start vllm

# watch it come up
journalctl -u vllm -f
A request has to clear two separate gates — the vLLM bind address and the EC2 security group — before it reaches the GPU.

Step 7 — Test the Endpoint From Your Laptop

Shell · curl from your local machine
curl http://1.2.3.4:8000/v1/chat/completions \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer token-abc123" \
  -d '{"model": "llama-3.1-8b", "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Explain KV caching in one sentence."}]}'
Python · same request via the OpenAI client
from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(
    base_url="http://1.2.3.4:8000/v1",
    api_key="token-abc123",
)

response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="llama-3.1-8b",
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Explain KV caching in one sentence."}],
    max_tokens=200,
)
print(response.choices[0].message.content)
💸
Stop the instance when you're done
A GPU instance bills by the second whether or not a request ever hits it. aws ec2 stop-instances --instance-ids i-0XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX before you close the laptop — a stopped instance keeps its EBS volume (and your downloaded model weights) but stops the compute meter. Terminate instead of stop only once you no longer need the disk.
🧠 Check your understanding
1. vLLM is bound to 0.0.0.0:8000 but a curl from your laptop times out. The security group has no rule for port 8000. What's the fix?
2. Why run vLLM under a systemd unit instead of just leaving the SSH session with the command running in the foreground?
3. You picked a stock Ubuntu AMI instead of a Deep Learning AMI to save a few GB of disk. What breaks first?
🔑
Key takeaways
1. Pick a G-series instance for single-model serving; save P-series for training or 70B+ models. 2. Use a Deep Learning AMI — fighting driver installs by hand is wasted time. 3. Exposing a server needs two independent gates: the bind address (--host 0.0.0.0) and the security group rule. 4. Never run an unauthenticated model endpoint on the open internet — always pass --api-key. 5. systemd, not a bare SSH session, is what makes a server production-durable. 6. Stop the instance the moment you're done — GPU-hours are the single biggest line item in an LLMOps budget.
